guide.title: About AAC files
guide.markdown:
### What is an AAC file?

AAC is a lossy audio codec developed by MPEG as MP3's successor; the name stands for Advanced Audio Coding. It is defined in MPEG-2 Part 7 and again in MPEG-4 Part 3. For a given bitrate it tends to sound better than MP3, so streaming, music downloads and phones lean on it.

The codec and the file are two things. AAC audio can sit inside an MP4 or QuickTime wrapper, which is what an .m4a file is. A standalone .aac file is different: it commonly carries ADTS framing, with no track information around it. The registered audio/aac media type covers that stream form, along with LATM/LOAS framing. Profiles such as LC, HE-AAC and HE-AAC v2 describe how the audio was coded, and a player has to support the profile as well as read the file.

A raw .aac stream can also start or end with ID3v1, ID3v2 or APE tags, which FFmpeg's aac demuxer reads along with the ADTS frames. The ADTS frame header holds a version bit that marks the stream as MPEG-2 or MPEG-4 AAC; FFmpeg's adts muxer writes 0, meaning MPEG-4, unless told otherwise. That bit is one reason a decoder built for one flavor can stumble on the other.

Because the same codec can live in either wrapper, moving between them is mostly a question of packaging.

### Programs that open AAC files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** VLC media player takes raw AAC as input and decodes the MPEG-4 version of AAC.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** FFmpeg includes an AAC decoder and its own AAC encoder.
- **Windows and Mac:** Adobe Audition imports AAC, including HE-AAC.

### AAC and MP4 compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .aac and audio/aac for a raw stream; .mp4 and video/mp4 for the container. Audio-only MPEG-4 files often use .m4a and the audio/mp4 type.
- **What each is**: AAC compresses sound. MP4, defined in ISO/IEC 14496-14 and first published in 2003, holds sound, video, subtitles and metadata in separate tracks.
- **Wrapper**: a raw .aac stream has none. Under the hood the container is ISO base media, an offshoot of QuickTime, and its track and timing data sit in nested boxes.
- **Video**: MP4 mostly holds H.264 video together with AAC audio, and other codecs, among them AV1, VP9, MP3 and Opus, can be stored in it as well. It does not need any video.

The wrapper changes, and so does the audio. On the page, FFmpeg decodes the AAC and encodes it again as AAC at 96 kbps inside an MP4. FFmpeg then makes a second pass that relocates the moov atom, its name for the index, to the front so players find the track information without reading the whole file. No picture is added, so you get an MP4 with sound only. The conversion runs entirely in your browser, so the recording is not uploaded anywhere, and each file in a batch becomes its own MP4.

### Other ways to convert AAC to MP4

Both methods copy the frames instead of encoding them again.

- **FFmpeg:** run `ffmpeg -i voice.aac -c:a copy voice-container.mp4`. Its documentation describes stream copy as no decoding or encoding, and its aac demuxer reads ADTS AAC, with any ID3v1/2 or APE tags in it. Nothing is re-encoded, so the audio keeps the bitrate it already had.
- **Bento4:** run `mp4mux --track aac:voice.aac voice-muxed.mp4`. Its documentation lists AAC input as ADTS format, and says that when you give no type before the colon, the type is inferred from the file extension. The output is the last name on the command line.

### Problems with AAC files

- **A file plays in one program and not another**: some decoders are built for MPEG-2 AAC only and cannot read the MPEG-4 variants. VLC accepts raw AAC input, so open the file there.
- **Renaming to .m4a did not help**: a new extension leaves the ADTS framing where it was and adds no MP4 wrapper. Only a real conversion changes the container.
- **The file is much larger once decoded**: AAC stores compressed audio, so an editor that unpacks it to raw samples uses far more space.
- **A ZIP does not shrink it**: AAC streams are already compressed, and zipping them usually saves little.

guide.title: About AI files
guide.markdown:
### What is an AI file?

A file ending in .ai is Illustrator's native document. Inside are paths, shapes and text drawn as vectors, along with layers, artboards and live effects, and placed raster images can sit among those objects. Logos, illustrations and print layouts are the usual jobs, and brushes, effects and transparency stay editable inside the file.

The format has been through changes: Illustrator 9 reworked it in 2000, and older files used PostScript. Newer files can carry a PDF-compatible copy beside Illustrator's private data, added when you save with the PDF-compatible option. That copy is how other software can draw the artwork without knowing Illustrator's internals.

Illustrator also lets an AI document mix vector objects with pixel images. Two AI files can look alike in a folder and differ inside: one carries the PDF-compatible rendition and the other does not. Third-party software can fail on a file saved without that rendition, because this converter draws the embedded PDF.

### Programs that open AI files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick lists the format as Illustrator CS2 and renders it to a picture instead of editing it.
- **Windows and Mac:** Adobe Illustrator opens native artwork with every object still editable, and it preserves the effects, brushes, layers and transparency stored in the document.
- **Linux:** Inkscape's manual says it imports AI artwork saved by Illustrator 9.0 or later, and some document features may not come across. The same manual notes that an import can open a dialog of options, and that some import formats depend on other programs installed on your computer.

### AI and JPEG compared

- **Extensions**: an Illustrator file ends in .ai; the picture ends in .jpg or .jpeg, two spellings of one format with the image/jpeg media type.
- **Kind of image**: an AI file is mostly vector artwork that can be scaled without losing sharpness. A JPEG is a raster, a fixed grid of pixels, at 8 bits for each color channel.
- **Compression**: JPEG is lossy. In its baseline mode a picture is cut into eight by eight pixel tiles. Each tile is run through a discrete cosine transform before entropy coding with Huffman tables. Progressive files differ by storing several passes, so a viewer can paint a low-detail picture early while downloading continues.
- **Origin**: the format is named for the committee that wrote it. Its core specification is ITU-T T.81, dated 1992, with ISO/IEC 10918-1 as the matching ISO text.
- **Quality**: programs usually expose a 0 to 100 slider, though one number can give different results from one program to the next.
- **Reach**: browsers all show JPEG, and cameras and scanners commonly produce it.
- **Transparency**: Illustrator keeps transparency. JPEG has none and cannot store layers.
- **Editing**: the AI file keeps layers, artboards and live text. A JPEG keeps none of that.

An editable document becomes a flat picture. The page takes the PDF stored inside your AI file, has PDF.js draw each page onto an opaque white background, and writes each one out as a JPEG. The size limits are in the FAQs below. An AI file with no PDF inside cannot be drawn, and the page tells you so.

### Other ways to convert AI to JPEG

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick brand.ai brand-proof.jpeg`. ImageMagick's format list shows AI as readable and says its PDF support requires Ghostscript.

### Problems with AI files

- **An error about a missing PDF**: Illustrator saved the file without its PDF-compatible copy. Reopen it there, turn the PDF-compatible saving option on, and convert the new copy.
- **An old file is refused**: a file from before Illustrator 9 was PostScript-based, so it has no embedded PDF to draw, and this page answers with the no-PDF message. Open it in Illustrator and save it again.
- **Part of the artwork is missing in Inkscape**: Inkscape imports only a subset of the features of some formats, and its manual lists AI files from Illustrator 9.0 onward.
- **Another program draws it wrong**: programs that read only the embedded PDF never see Illustrator's native objects. For editing, use Illustrator.
- **An older Illustrator opens it badly**: Adobe recommends opening artwork in the version that saved it or a newer one.
- **Linked images are missing**: they stay external unless Include Linked Files was selected while saving.

guide.title: About AMR files
guide.markdown:
### What is an AMR file?

Adaptive Multi-Rate, abbreviated AMR, began as an ETSI speech codec for GSM and was later taken up by 3GPP for 3G networks. The codec is tuned for speech and produces tiny files, so phones favor it for voice recordings and voice messages.

A .amr file normally holds the narrowband codec, sampled at 8 kHz and split into 20-millisecond frames with eight speech modes from 4.75 to 12.2 kbps. AMR-WB is its own codec at 16 kHz, with nine wideband modes running from 6.6 to 23.85 kbps. The file starts with a text signature: the characters #!AMR and a line break for narrowband, and #!AMR-WB for wideband. Each stored speech frame then begins with a one-octet header holding a frame type, a quality bit and padding, and the last octet of the speech bits is zero-padded for alignment. A quality bit set to 0 marks a severely damaged frame. A frame that was lost or never transmitted is stored as NO_DATA, and the wideband file can also use SPEECH_LOST. RFC 4867, from April 2007, covers AMR files and their RTP transport, and it registers audio/AMR for narrowband.

You usually meet an AMR file as a recording that came off an older phone, and then find that your computer cannot play it or your editor will not import it. Audacity imports WAV, so a WAV copy gets around that.

Archivists at the Library of Congress list WAVE among recommended formats for audio collections, which suits a recording you mean to keep.

### Programs that open AMR files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** FFmpeg is a command-line tool with decoders for AMR narrowband and AMR wideband.

### AMR and WAV compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .amr and audio/AMR for narrowband AMR; .wav and audio/wav or audio/x-wav for WAV.
- **Kind of format**: AMR names a speech codec, whereas WAV is a RIFF wrapper that can hold several encodings, usually linear PCM but sometimes compressed ones.
- **Compression**: AMR is lossy and tuned for speech. PCM in WAV is uncompressed.
- **Frames**: an AMR file is a run of 20-millisecond speech frames, each with its own small header. A WAV stores a continuous stream of samples, so the frame structure disappears in the conversion.
- **Bandwidth**: AMR suits a voice and little else. WAV can hold much wider audio, but a WAV made from AMR still carries only what the AMR kept.
- **Limits and metadata**: a WAV has a 4 GB size limit, and very large recordings may need RF64 rather than the original RIFF size fields. Broadcast WAVE adds production and preservation metadata, and since extension chunks and the standard INFO chunks hold different information, programs treat them differently.

What changes in this conversion is the storage, not the sound. The page runs FFmpeg in a worker and writes 16-bit PCM. The result is a plain waveform. Audacity opens nearly every WAV, all PCM variants included, with no extra library, but a WAV with a recorder's proprietary compression is a case where Audacity recommends its FFmpeg library. It does not reverse the speech compression, and raising the sampling rate in another program afterward cannot put missing frequencies back.

### Other ways to convert AMR to WAV

- **FFmpeg:** run `ffmpeg -i memo.amr memo-edit.wav`. FFmpeg's codec documentation lists decoders for AMR narrowband and wideband, and says the AMR-NB one is built into FFmpeg itself.

### Problems with AMR files

- **The sound is thin or tinny**: that is the codec. A narrowband recording cannot supply the wider frequency range of an AMR-WB source, because the two use different sampling rates.
- **You are not sure what it is**: check the first bytes. A narrowband file begins with #!AMR and a line break, and a wideband file with #!AMR-WB.
- **Renaming did not work**: AMR and AMR-WB signatures differ, and changing an extension cannot change the encoded speech.
- **The WAV is far larger than the AMR**: AMR packs speech into a few kilobits a second, while a WAV holds every sample as uncompressed PCM, so the file grows even though no detail is added.
- **The recording is cut off**: a partial transfer from the phone gives a partial recording. This page usually still turns the part that arrived into a shorter WAV, but copy the file across again for the whole memo.

guide.title: About AV1 files
guide.markdown:
### What is an AV1 file?

AV1 stands for AOMedia Video 1. It is a video codec, not a complete movie format. The Alliance for Open Media developed its bitstream and decoding specification, and the Library of Congress describes it as an open, royalty-free video coding format. The public release of the specification was announced on March 28, 2018.

An AV1 bitstream is organized into units called OBUs. Its registered media type is video/av1, and it supports full-resolution chroma setups such as 4:4:4. A .av1 file on this page's input side is that bare stream: video only, with no audio track and nothing wrapped around it. Most of the AV1 you meet sits inside an MP4 or WebM file.

AV1 has no required file extension, so the ending alone cannot tell you the framing. A raw stream of OBUs and an AV1 image container are different inputs, and FFmpeg documents them as separate formats. AV1 encoding can take longer than older codecs because its compression process is complex. You get a .av1 file from an encoder such as aomenc, or from a tool that writes out a video stream on its own.

### Programs that open AV1 files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** FFmpeg supports AV1 through external libraries, among them libaom, libdav1d, librav1e and libsvtav1.

### AV1 and MP4 compared

- **What each is**: AV1 is a codec. MP4, defined in ISO/IEC 14496-14, is a container that can hold H.264, H.265 or AV1 video along with audio.
- **Sound**: a .av1 stream has none, so an MP4 made from it has none either.
- **Reach**: H.264 is the video most phones, editors and upload forms handle. AV1 depends on a decoder, which some devices lack.
- **Playback**: a container that FFmpeg or a player accepts does not guarantee a decoder for the video inside it.
- **Extensions**: .av1 has no required extension; .mp4 is the container's.
- **Safety of the file**: a standard MP4 holds its index data in one place, so an interrupted write can leave a file that no player opens.

Both the codec and the wrapper change. Your browser decodes the AV1 with its built-in decoder, and the page writes H.264 into the MP4. The picture is capped at 1920 pixels along its longer edge and 30 frames per second. Frames are removed from a faster clip, which keeps the running time, and since the encoder needs even sizes, a side with an odd pixel count gets one pixel trimmed. All of this runs in your browser, so the video never leaves your device, and each file in a batch gets its own MP4.

That also explains the wait: the page decodes, re-encodes and scales entirely on your device, and several files run one after another. The MP4 has no sound.

### Other ways to convert AV1 to MP4

- **GPAC MP4Box:** run `MP4Box -add scene.av1 scene-av1.mp4`. This keeps AV1 inside the MP4. The GPAC article says to add `:fps=1000` if the stream carries no timing, and `:fmt=obu` if the extension is not recognized. It accepts OBU, IVF and Annex B framing, and it does not accept WebM.
- **FFmpeg, stream copy:** run `ffmpeg -i clip.av1 -c:v copy -an clip-copy.mp4`. Copying skips decoding and encoding, so the AV1 is untouched, and the MP4 still needs an AV1 decoder to play.

### Problems with AV1 files

- **"Your browser can't decode AV1"**: your device has no AV1 decoder for the browser to use. Try a recent Chrome or Edge on a different computer, or use FFmpeg.
- **The file will not play**: the suffix does not tell you the framing. A raw OBU stream and an IVF file differ, so name the framing yourself when you import it.

- **An audio editor shows nothing**: an MP4 without audio cannot provide an audio track to an editor, and a .av1 stream never had one.
- **Encoding takes a while**: AV1's compression process is complex, so a longer clip takes longer.

guide.title: About CDR files
guide.markdown:
### What is a CDR file?

Drawings made in CorelDRAW are stored as CDR, the program's default format. Corel calls the format primarily vector, meaning shapes, curves and text that stay crisp at any size, though a drawing can also contain bitmaps and vector effects. Saving can compress the bitmaps and graphic objects. The file can carry reference properties such as a title and a subject, and embedded fonts, within their permissions.

To share a drawing with someone on an older release, the Save As dialog offers earlier CDR versions. Corel says CorelDRAW files do not work backwards; saving to an earlier version can change newer effects or limit editing.

A CDR usually arrives from a designer, a sign shop, a print vendor or a client who works in CorelDRAW. It is the working file, so a PNG is what people want when they need to show or place the design instead of editing it.

### Programs that open CDR files

- **Windows and Mac:** CorelDRAW created the format and opens it natively. Double-click a file, or use File > Open.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** LibreOffice Draw lists Corel Draw (*.cdr) among the formats it can import.

### CDR and PNG compared

- **Extensions**: .cdr for the drawing; .png and image/png for the picture.
- **What each holds**: a CDR keeps editable shapes, text and effects, whereas a PNG keeps one flat picture made of pixels.
- **Scaling**: drawings scale without loss, but a PNG turns soft when enlarged, so choose the final size at export.
- **Compression**: PNG always compresses without loss, through the DEFLATE method, so the picture matches what the program drew.
- **Structure**: a PNG opens with a fixed signature and continues as chunks: an IHDR chunk describes the image, IDAT chunks hold its compressed pixels, and an IEND chunk ends the file.
- **Bit depth**: indexed, grayscale and truecolor PNGs can use between 1 and 16 bits per sample.
- **Reach**: every major browser displays PNG, and it carries no known royalty-bearing patents.
- **Animation**: the current specification includes animated PNG, with a default image shown by software that cannot play the animation.
- **Transparency**: PNG supports an optional alpha channel, so a see-through background is possible if the export is set up for it.
- **Editing**: all object structure is gone in a PNG. Keep the CDR as the master.

What matters is the program that draws the file, since it decides how the drawing looks as a picture. Image decoding on this page belongs to the browser itself, and for a CDR you should expect "Image decode failed." instead of a picture, so use one of the methods below.

### Other ways to convert CDR to PNG

- **CorelDRAW, single export:** choose File > Export (Ctrl+E on Windows, Cmd+E on Mac), select PNG in the Save as type list, click Export, then set the options in the Export to PNG dialog and click OK. Corel's Export command provides raster formats, while Save As offers only vector ones.
- **CorelDRAW, asset export:** choose File > Export For > Multiple Files, add the objects or page in the Export docker, pick PNG for each and export.
- **LibreOffice Draw:** open the CDR, then use File > Export, choose PNG and set the options. The PNG dialog covers compression and interlacing, plus width, height and resolution of the picture, and the help page for it lists them.

### Problems with CDR files

- **The page shows an error**: its decoder is the browser's own, and it reports "Image decode failed." for this file. Export from CorelDRAW or LibreOffice Draw instead.
- **An older CorelDRAW rejects the file**: ask whoever made it for an earlier-version copy. Newer effects may look different in that copy.
- **A renamed file stays unreadable**: calling the file .png leaves the drawing data untouched, and image viewers reject it.
- **The text looks wrong**: the drawing may use fonts that were not embedded, and a program without them swaps in others. Ask the sender to embed the fonts, which CorelDRAW allows subject to font permissions, and install them before you export.
- **You want to keep editing**: a PNG is a flat picture with no objects left in it. Keep the CDR, and export a new PNG whenever the design changes.
- **The PNG is blurry**: it holds a fixed number of pixels. Export again at a larger size from the program.

guide.title: About DDS files
guide.markdown:
### What is a DDS file?

DDS stands for DirectDraw Surface. It is Microsoft's texture file format, and games and 3D tools use it to store textures. A DDS can hold plain pixels or compressed texture data, which commonly means the DXT and BC block formats that a graphics card reads directly.

A single DDS often holds more than one image: a mipmap chain of ever smaller copies of the top surface, cube maps, or volume textures. The extra header introduced for Direct3D 10 and 11 brings texture arrays and names pixel formats that the first header's structure could not describe. The properties list also includes an alpha channel.

The older header describes pixel layouts such as plain RGB and the DXT1 to DXT5 block-compressed forms, which have the broadest tool support. You meet DDS files when you unpack a game, work with mods or materials, or receive assets from a 3D artist. Photo programs and browsers rarely open them, so a JPG is the quick way to see what a texture looks like.

### Programs that open DDS files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP gained built-in DDS support in version 2.10.10, and its release notes say it can load and export DDS out of the box.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick documents DDS reading and writing, with options for DXT compression and mipmaps.

### DDS and JPG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .dds for the texture; .jpg or .jpeg and image/jpeg for the picture.
- **Content**: a DDS can hold several surfaces. A JPG holds one image and cannot store layers.
- **Compression**: a DDS can store GPU-ready block data. JPEG is lossy and aimed at photographs. A baseline JPEG divides the image into 8x8 squares, transforms each square with a discrete cosine transform, then compresses the coefficients using Huffman tables. Block edges become visible at low quality settings.
- **Transparency and depth**: a DDS can have an alpha channel. JPEG has none and stores 8 bits per color channel.
- **Variants**: legacy headers cover plain RGB and DXT1 to DXT5. The DX10 extension adds more formats, and some readers reject it.
- **Modes**: progressive JPEG paints a blurry first pass, then sharpens as the remaining data arrives.
- **Origin**: the Joint Photographic Experts Group started in 1986, and its core standard appeared as ITU-T T.81 in 1992. Cameras and scanners ship with JPEG built in, in most cases.
- **Quality**: JPEG offers an adjustable 0 to 100 scale, and its numbers are not comparable across programs.

A texture turns into an ordinary flat picture. The browser runs ImageMagick as WebAssembly, pulls one image from the DDS and saves it as a JPG. The page sets no quality value, and it refuses a picture over about 537 megapixels. See-through pixels in the texture are lost, because a JPG cannot hold them.

Treat the JPG as a preview. It does not keep the mipmap levels, cube map faces or array elements a renderer uses, and it cannot stand in for the original texture.

### Other ways to convert DDS to JPG

- **Microsoft DirectXTex:** run `texconv -ft jpg material.dds`. The `-ft` option sets the output file type and accepts jpg and jpeg. The `--ignore-mips` option leaves the mipmap levels out.
- **GIMP:** open the DDS and export it as a JPEG. In GIMP's JPEG export dialog the quality starts at 85, and the saved file holds neither transparency nor layers.
- **ImageMagick:** run `magick material.dds material-preview.jpg`. The formats page marks DDS as readable and writable.

### Problems with DDS files

- **A reader rejects the file**: a few readers cannot parse the DX10 extension, whereas an older RGB or DXT1-to-DXT5 header opens in more tools.
- **The file is invalid**: a header shorter than 128 bytes, or 148 with the DX10 extension, is truncated. Copy the file again.
- **Scan lines look corrupted**: a wrong pitch value makes a reader misjudge where each row starts. Microsoft advises computing the pitch from the stored format.
- **Only one picture came out**: ImageMagick reads a single image from a multi-surface texture, so the other surfaces do not appear.
- **Transparency disappeared**: JPG has no alpha. Convert to PNG if the see-through areas matter.
- **You need every mip level or face**: use a texture-aware tool such as texconv, and keep the DDS as the source.

guide.title: About DNG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a DNG file?

Adobe published DNG, short for Digital Negative, in 2004 as an open raw format meant to replace the many proprietary ones with one documented design. The Library of Congress lists it as a subtype of TIFF 6.0 and notes that a file can comply with both DNG and TIFF/EP. The recommended extension is .dng.

Two kinds of DNG exist. A raw DNG holds mosaiced sensor data, typically from a Bayer array. A linear DNG is a rarer variety that holds RGB image data, usually demosaiced, which means the demosaicing choices cannot be redone later. The raw samples can be packed with lossless JPEG compression, and a DNG may contain an Exif metadata block, and it also uses IPTC and XMP tags plus proprietary tags for camera converters.

People use DNG for archiving raw photos, for raw files from some phones and cameras, and for passing raw files between editors. The Library of Congress accepts it for digital photographs and graphic images.

You meet DNG files in a photo library or when a photographer sends raw files. Most people cannot open one in a browser or a document viewer, and a PDF is a common way to show a raw photo to someone who does not have a raw editor.

### Programs that open DNG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** darktable includes DNG in the extensions it considers for import, and it reads raw files through the RawSpeed library. Apart from Fujifilm X-Trans cameras, it does not decode images from cameras with non-Bayer sensors.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick reads DNG when you give the dng: prefix.

### DNG and PDF compared

- **Extensions**: .dng for the raw file; .pdf for the document.
- **What they hold**: a DNG holds data to develop a photo, possibly the raw sensor mosaic. A PDF holds a finished page.
- **Compression**: a DNG can use lossless JPEG for its raw samples, whereas this page places the picture in the PDF as a PNG.
- **Imaging model**: PDF draws with a model inherited from PostScript, independent of device and resolution. Lossless Flate compression and JPEG are both available for the images inside.
- **Media types**: application/pdf for the document, and .dng for the raw file's recommended extension.
- **Metadata**: Exif tags in a DNG can sit in a separate directory, which the specification prefers over the TIFF/EP one.
- **Page**: a PDF has pages. A DNG has none.
- **Editing**: a DNG supports re-developing the photo. A PDF cannot.

A raw file turns into a picture placed on a page. In the browser ImageMagick reads one image from the DNG, and the page wraps it in a one-page PDF. The sheet matches the picture, counting each pixel as a point, and has no margins. Each DNG yields a separate PDF, and the work happens in your browser, so the photo is not uploaded anywhere. The page sets no quality value, and a picture beyond roughly 537 megapixels is refused.

The picture is embedded without lossy compression, but that does not preserve the DNG. Only the finished picture is kept, so develop the photo first if tone, crop and color matter.

### Other ways to convert DNG to PDF

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick dng:archive-photo.dng archive-proof.pdf`. The ImageMagick formats page marks DNG as read-only and says it requires an explicit specifier such as dng:image.dng. It also marks PDF as readable and writable and says writing it requires Ghostscript.

### Problems with DNG files

- **The file will not decode**: a linear DNG already holds demosaiced data, so it is not the same as an untouched sensor mosaic. A reader may not support every sensor pattern, and darktable documents its limits for non-Bayer sensors.
- **"Compression can't be decoded here"**: the raw reader cannot decode that kind of DNG. Use the camera maker's software and export a TIFF or JPEG.
- **The photo can look flat at first**: a raw file holds unprocessed sensor data, and the picture you see comes from how it is developed. If the look matters, develop it in your editor first.
- **The PDF will not look like your editor's version**: the finished picture, not the raw data, goes into the PDF, so settle the look first.
- **The page size is wrong**: this page follows the image size. For A4 or Letter with margins, place the photo in a layout program.

guide.title: About DOCX files
guide.markdown:
### What is a DOCX file?

Microsoft Word has saved new documents as DOCX by default since Word 2007. The file is a ZIP package built on the Open Packaging Conventions. WordprocessingML carries the text and its formatting, and styles, images, properties and relationships are kept as separate parts. The format is specified in ECMA-376 and ISO/IEC 29500.

That structure is why pulling out only the main XML part does not give you the full document. A resume, a letter or a report keeps its text, tables and images together in the one package.

People send DOCX files for letters, reports, contracts and resumes, and tracked changes and comments live inside them. A JPEG is what you want when a form takes only pictures, when you are posting a page on a site that does not accept documents, or when you want a page to look the same everywhere without anyone needing a word processor.

### Programs that open DOCX files

- **Windows and Mac:** Microsoft Word introduced the format and has made it the default for new documents ever since Word 2007.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** LibreOffice Writer imports Word .docx files, and its help notes that a DOCX opened there may lose some formatting attributes.

### DOCX and JPEG compared

- **Extensions**: .docx for the document; .jpg and .jpeg, which are the same format, for the image.
- **What each holds**: a DOCX holds editable text, styles, tables and images. A JPEG holds one picture of a page.
- **Pages**: a DOCX flows into as many pages as its text needs. A JPEG is one page, so a long document gives many files.
- **Compression**: JPEG is lossy and made for photographs, with quality usually set on a 0 to 100 scale. It stores 8 bits per color channel and cannot hold transparency.
- **Reach**: every major browser displays JPEG, and the registered media type is image/jpeg.

What changes in this conversion is the page itself. docx-preview lays the document out inside a sandbox where every node is built, and each page is drawn at double its point size, which makes US Letter 1224 by 1584 pixels. No side of the image passes 4096 pixels. A page breaks where the document says to, and where text runs past the height of a page, between paragraphs or table rows, with the header and footer repeated.

Word is not the program drawing the pages. Fonts your browser lacks fall back to its default.

### Other ways to convert DOCX to JPEG

- **Microsoft Word and ImageMagick:** in Word choose File > Save a Copy > Browse, pick PDF as the type and save. Then run `magick statement.pdf statement-page.jpg`. The PDF comes from Word's own layout, and ImageMagick needs Ghostscript to read PDF.
- **LibreOffice Writer and ImageMagick:** open the DOCX in Writer, pick File > Export As > Export as PDF, and save the PDF beside it. After that run `magick report.pdf report-page.jpg`. The ImageMagick formats page marks PDF as readable and writable.

### Problems with DOCX files

- **The text looks different in another program**: another word processor can drop some formatting while importing.
- **List numbers use the wrong digits**: the capture drops CSS counters, so the page writes list numbers out as text, and CJK or Hebrew numbering turns into decimal digits. Check those lists before you send the JPEG.
- **Pictures do not show**: the sandbox builds every node itself, so a picture that the file links to but does not hold loads nothing. Embed it in Word and save a copy.
- **The page size is not what you expected**: a file with no page size is drawn as US Letter, and that fallback has one-inch margins. Set A4 or another size in Word first.
- **A table breaks across pages**: its header rows are marked in the file as w:tblHeader, and that mark is what makes them repeat.
- **Embedded HTML is missing**: the page leaves out any altChunk, the HTML that a file can carry inside it. Open the document in Word to see it, or export a PDF from there.
- **Small print looks soft**: a page is a fixed grid of pixels, so fine print blurs when you enlarge it. A PDF export from Word keeps text sharp at any size.
- **Page breaks moved**: this page does not use Word's own layout. For the exact page breaks, export a PDF from Word and turn that into JPEGs.

guide.title: About FLAC files
guide.markdown:
### What is a FLAC file?

The name FLAC expands to Free Lossless Audio Codec. Integer PCM goes in, a smaller stream comes out, and decoding returns the identical samples. Anyone can read the specification, and the reference code is open source. A native FLAC stream is labeled audio/flac, and the format description was issued as RFC 9639 in December 2024.

Channel counts run from one to eight and bit depths from 4 to 32. FLAC metadata can include seek points, pictures and Vorbis comments. Storage corruption can make a frame fail its checksum, since lossless encoding gives no protection against it.

Because it is lossless, FLAC is also a good source to convert from: the encoder starts with the full audio, not a file that has already been through a lossy pass. The format reference names music archiving, audiophile listening and CD backups as typical uses.

### Programs that open FLAC files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Audacity imports FLAC with its built-in importer, which also covers Ogg Vorbis, MP2, WAV and AIFF, so no FFmpeg add-on is needed.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** VLC media player counts FLAC among its input formats and audio codecs, and AAC appears on its features page too.

### FLAC and AAC compared

- **Extensions and media types**: FLAC files end in .flac and use audio/flac; a raw AAC stream ends in .aac.
- **Compression**: FLAC is lossless. AAC is lossy, so it discards detail to make the file smaller.
- **Channels and depth**: FLAC goes up to eight channels and 32-bit samples.
- **Wrapper**: AAC can be a raw .aac stream or sit inside an MP4 container.
- **Support**: some devices lack a FLAC decoder, while AAC is widely supported.
- **Use**: AAC serves streaming audio and music downloads, audio in MP4 videos and mobile devices. FLAC serves music archiving and lossless backups of CDs.
- **Players**: VLC media player, Apple Music, Windows Media Player and any web browser open AAC.

The big change is that lossless audio turns lossy. In a worker, FFmpeg built for WebAssembly encodes the audio to AAC at 192 kbps with its own encoder and skips video streams. The page passes no option for sample rate or channel layout, so FFmpeg decides them. Several files can be chosen at once. Files are handled in turn, and every one is downloaded separately as an .aac, with no ZIP. The page sets no size limit or timeout of its own, so a long track takes as long as your device needs. Your original file is not changed, because you download a new copy. Hold on to the FLAC if you will want full quality later.

### Other ways to convert FLAC to AAC

- **FFmpeg:** run `ffmpeg -i album.flac -c:a aac -b:a 192k album-listen.aac`. The FFmpeg codec documentation describes its native AAC encoder as the default one, and the adts muxer writes a single AAC stream.
- **Audacity and qaac:** qaac takes WAV, so first export a WAV from Audacity: open the FLAC, choose File > Export Audio and pick WAV, whose default encoding is Signed 16-bit PCM. The dialog can export the whole project or only a selection, so you can bridge just the part you need. Then run `qaac --adts -V 90 bridge.wav -o alternate.aac`. The qaac wiki describes `--adts` as ADTS output for AAC only and `-V` as a True VBR quality scale from 0 to 127, with -V90 as the default for the LC profile. It is a Windows console tool and needs Apple Application Support.

### Problems with FLAC files

- **It will not play on a phone**: a player without a FLAC decoder cannot open the file at all. Android documents native FLAC playback that is narrower than the format itself, which makes an AAC copy the safer pick for phones.
- **A file stops partway**: a bad disk or interrupted download can break a frame's checksum, and FLAC cannot repair that. Transfer the file again.
- **The FLAC came from an MP3 or AAC**: such a FLAC is only a bigger file, and the earlier loss stays. Converting it to AAC adds a second lossy pass.
- **The FLAC takes a lot of room**: the format reference says FLAC typically halves uncompressed audio, which is still bulky beside a lossy copy.
- **You need full quality**: AAC is lossy, so pick FLAC again if you need the audio for editing or archiving.

faqs.question: Is converting FLAC to AIFF lossless?

faqs.question: The AIFF file is huge next to my FLAC. Is that normal?

faqs.question: AIFF versus WAV: which should I pick?

faqs.question: Does AIFF support compressed audio?
faqs.answer: AIFF-C, an extension of the family, does. This page writes plain AIFF with uncompressed PCM. A program reading AIFF-C needs a decoder for the actual encoding.

faqs.question: Can I convert AIFF back to FLAC?

faqs.question: Why does my FLAC fail to convert?

guide.title: About FLAC files
guide.markdown:
### What is a FLAC file?

Free Lossless Audio Codec, or FLAC, squeezes integer PCM audio and returns every sample on decoding, since nothing about the samples is discarded. Its specification is public and the reference code is open source; December 2024 saw the format description published as RFC 9639. A native FLAC stream carries the media type audio/flac.

A FLAC can hold between one and eight channels at depths from four to 32 bits per sample. Seek points, embedded pictures and Vorbis comments live in its metadata blocks. Lossless coding cannot stop a damaged frame from failing its checksum when the storage corrupts it.

A FLAC makes a good source for a conversion, since the converter begins with the complete audio and not with something a lossy pass has already trimmed. Bit depth matters for this pair, because the AIFF written here is 16-bit. The format reference lists music archiving, audiophile listening and CD rips kept lossless as typical uses, and says FLAC typically shrinks files to about half the size of uncompressed audio.

### Programs that open FLAC files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Audacity imports FLAC with its built-in importer, so the optional FFmpeg library is not needed.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** VLC media player lists FLAC as both an input format and an audio codec.

### FLAC and AIFF compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .flac with audio/flac on one side, .aiff with audio/aiff or audio/x-aiff on the other.
- **Compression**: FLAC is lossless compression. AIFF often carries uncompressed linear PCM, and its AIFF-C extension can hold compressed audio.
- **Size**: expect the AIFF to dwarf the FLAC, because uncompressed PCM takes more storage than a packed copy.
- **Support**: Audacity reads FLAC directly and imports most AIFF files, all PCM variants among them, with no optional FFmpeg library.
- **Metadata**: FLAC stores Vorbis comments and pictures, while AIFF can add named chunks holding author, copyright and annotation text.
- **Use**: AIFF turns up in masters and intermediate recordings made by professional audio users, while FLAC turns up in music archives.
- **Origin**: Apple built AIFF as an audio wrapper from Electronic Arts' IFF family. Its AIFF 1.3 specification carries the date January 4, 1989.

Two things change: how the audio is stored, and on this page the bit depth. FFmpeg built for WebAssembly decodes your FLAC, leaves out any video stream, and writes signed 16-bit big-endian PCM inside an AIFF wrapper. The page passes no sample-rate or channel option, which leaves both to FFmpeg. A FLAC at 16 bits comes through sample for sample, and a deeper one is cut to 16. You download a new copy and your original stays untouched; a long file takes whatever time your device needs.

### Other ways to convert FLAC to AIFF

- **FFmpeg:** run `ffmpeg -i master.flac master-work.aiff`, and FFmpeg picks the AIFF muxer from the extension. FFmpeg's general documentation lists AIFF muxing and demuxing, as well as FLAC.
- **SoX:** run `sox master.flac master-working.aiff`. The SoX manual says the file type comes from the file extension, so the .aiff name in the command is what selects the output format. Its format page says FLAC support is optional and that its AIFF support does not include multiple audio chunks.

### Problems with FLAC files

- **It will not open in my program**: not every program reads FLAC. Convert to AIFF here, or open the file in VLC or Audacity.
- **The file is cut off**: storage errors can break a frame's checksum, and lossless coding cannot undo damage to the file. Download or copy it again from wherever it came from, then convert the fresh copy.
- **The FLAC was made from an MP3**: the detail that MP3 discarded is gone, and the AIFF stays just as limited.
- **A player rejects an AIFF-C file**: its compression scheme may be one the player lacks, because the family name alone proves nothing about support. This page writes plain PCM.
- **ID3 tags are absent in the AIFF**: FFmpeg's AIFF muxer writes ID3v2 tags only when its write_id3v2 option is enabled, and the command used here does not enable it. Raw PCM muxers in FFmpeg store no metadata at all.
- **The AIFF is huge**: nothing in it is compressed. Store the FLAC and use the AIFF only while editing.
